svg.title: Digestion & enzymes
svg.desc: The digestive route: Mouth: chewing and amylase. Oesophagus: moves food to the stomach. Stomach: acid, protease and mixing. Pancreas: supplies digestive enzymes. Small intestine: digestion and absorption. Large intestine: absorbs water. Egestion: undigested food leaves. Excretion: metabolic waste leaves. Enzyme products: Amylase: starch → sugars. Made in salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine. Protease: protein → amino acids. Made in stomach, pancreas and small intestine. Lipase: lipid → glycerol + fatty acids. Made in pancreas and small intestine. Specific active sites: Enzymes are reusable protein catalysts. Substrate fits a complementary active site, like a lock and key. Warming increases collisions up to an optimum. Cold slows the reaction. Excess heat or extreme pH can denature the enzyme: the active site changes shape, so substrate cannot fit. Bile & absorbed products: Liver: makes bile. Gall bladder: stores it. Alkaline bile neutralises stomach acid. Emulsification: smaller fat droplets give more surface area for lipase. Bile is not an enzyme. Absorbed products build new molecules. Glucose can be used in respiration. Food tests: Benedict’s: reducing sugar gives a coloured precipitate after heating in a water bath. Iodine: starch turns blue-black. Biuret: protein turns purple. Sudan III: lipid forms a red oil layer. Use separate samples and positive/negative controls. Wear goggles and heat safely. Amylase & pH practical: Vary buffer pH. Control temperature, enzyme/starch concentrations and volumes. Test samples on fresh iodine every 30 seconds. When starch is digested, iodine stays orange-brown. Repeat. For the same starch quantity, relative rate = 1/time. Shorter sampling intervals improve endpoint resolution.
